chapter: Apollo Bar, Apollo managers and Harlem nightlife
title: Junior Raglin, his dirty shirts and Hinton's gin delivery
summary: Whaley and Hinton tell stories about bassist Junior Raglin, including bringing gin to Hinton at Cab Calloway's engagement.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Did you know Junior Ragland. He was one of the beautiful people that was in Duke's band.
I'll tell you about Junior, Junior would never put on a clean shirt.

Always a dirtyshirt. I said do you see Duke out there immaculate, and look at you. I said why don't you -- shucks, I remember one day, we were supposed to play the United States Bond Hour, and Ragland and Duke had rehearsed together, they were going to play a number and we went to -- after rehearsal we went to this club and I said 'Ragland, hey don't drink too much because you got to get up in the morning.' Shucks, you know, Ragland got drunk and everytime I'd look up the waiter was saying 'that man over there ordered a drink.' I said 'don't give him anymore.' So went to sleep, got up in the morning, we couldn't wake Junior Ragland up. We put him on some cold water, that didn't do him any good.
Junior was out. He sure was.

He was a natural bass player and a natural musician. Not to jump into your history but I knew him and we loved each other. He loved me dearly and I loved him, respect him as a bass player. But he was, as you say, he hadn't had the kind of background that we had about cleanliness

and his feet was always bare, he wore house shoes and Duke hired him because Duke was looking for talent and surely, Junior was a talent, so he hired and I can remember Junior used to bring me, he'd drink a drink called Junior Flip where you took gin and cherry juice and put it together and this one particular year during the wartimes Cab Calloway was at the Park Sheraton Hotel which is at 56th and 7th Avenue and Duke was at the Zanzibar at 49th Street and Broadway and during our intermission, they had intermission, Junior loving me so and respecting me so, he would fix a quart pitcher of this gin and put cherry juice in it and put a cover over it and in his house shoes, he would walk from 49th and Broadway up to 56th and 7th Avenue with this gin in a pitcher with a napkin over the top of it.

And I'm playing this very sedity club with Cab Calloway, Cab was most dignified in those days and his band was very dignified. We had white tails on and we were playing on the roof, the garden roof of the Park Sheraton Hotel and Junior Ragland would -- not up the service entrance, but right up the main entrance and he'd come up there on the elevator and he's a huge young man, he had a big bulk of a body and that very sad looking face, looked like it loved everybody like -- what are those dogs in Switzerland that people attribute to carrying the rum around their shoulders -- St. Bernard and he had that sort of St. Bernard dog look on his face and this huge

body and here he comes up on the elevator with this quart of gin and he gets off and he walks in this club and the maitre'd says sir, may I do something for you. He says no everything is cool. I just want to take this up to Milt Hinton and the maitre'd is trying to tell him that he should come up through the service entrance and he just walks right straight through the club and walks up to the bandstand and sits his quart of gin down on the bandstand with all the customers dancing and Cab Calloway looks at me, get your damn friends out of here.
That was the kind of beautiful human being that Junior Ragland Ragland was, besides being a truly great bass player.
